> Is there a way to add a variable to the R workspace, using the high  
> level
> API of the Rengine class, but to add this variable into a specific
> environment?
>

No. The REngine API is intended to support that at some point [via  
REXPEnvironment.assign(name, value)] but currently the REngine API is  
not yet supported by JRI.

A work-around is to assign it into the global environment as a  
temporary variable and then copy it using an explicit assignment call  
in R.


> Please tell me if it is a wrong place for asking this question.
>

It's the right place, but please add more details in the future as of  
which package you are talking about, version etc. since this list is  
for all Java related packages.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
Graham,

On Mar 10, 2009, at 9:51 , Graham Etherington wrote:

> Hi Simon,
> Sorry for being unclear. I'll reword my message.
>
> Is there a way to pass R objects, such as hclust objects between JRI/ 
> Java classes (obviously, as some sort of Java/JRI data type). I have  
> a load of Java classes and methods that use JRI to carry out various  
> functions, to produce distance matrices, carry out clustering and  
> display the results graphically. I want to keep each step separate  
> in order for a user to choose which methods are performed next, so I  
> have a Java class which produces distance matrices, then I pass the  
> distance matrix to a Java class which does clustering, then I want  
> to pass the result of the clustering to a Java class which displays  
> the clustering graphically. All the classes use JRI. Sometimes I  
> might want to go straight from producing a distance matrix to  
> displaying the result graphically (eg a phylogenetic tree).


I think now I know what you mean.

First, let me explain the principles, then I'll get back to your  
underlying question.

R and Java are languages with completely different paradigms and  
native types (R has no scalars, float, entirely different class  
system, ...). This means that you cannot just simply map an R object  
to a Java object and vice versa. Therefore there is a two-level  
approach:

1) when either side touches (requests) an object on the other side, a  
transparent "proxy" object is created on the local side. For example  
when Java requests a result from R, it creates a proxy object in Java  
that is nothing but a pointer to the R object. It cannot be used in  
Java in any way since Java has no actual access to the R object.  
However, it can be used back in R to refer to the object that Java  
requested. The same is true the other way round (when R requests a  
Java object...).

2) in order to be able to use the foreign object in any way beyond  
just passing it back, it needs to be converted into a native object in  
the requesting system. For example if you request 1:10 from R, you  
need to convert the result into int[] in Java. rJava/JRI provides  
convertors in both ways with varying completeness. Note that this  
conversion is potentially lossy, because some constructs cannot be  
directly represented in the given language (e.g. R function has no  
corresponding representation in Java).

Now to your problem.

When you are using eval, you can tell JRI which level you want to get  
back using the "convert" parameter in the eval method. By default it  
is true, i.e., the result will be converted to native Java  
representation. This is usually what users want since the point of  
getting it to Java is to be able to extract the data from the object.  
However, in your case you want to pass the object back to R as-is,  
which is only possible if you get a reference instead of the native  
object - hence you have to use convert=false. You can always convert  
the reference into its native Java representation by using new  
REXP(r.getEngine(), r.xp, true).

Now, ideally you should be able to specify a function and its  
arguments as objects (e.g. r.evalFunction("foo", bar, bla)). However,  
JRI does not have an API for that (yet?), so what you have to do is to  
temporarily assign it. In fact R is smart enough to not make a copy,  
so it shouldn't be an issue - it's just a minor annoyance.

So the whole thing would look somewhat like this:

REXP r = c.eval("myFunction()", false);
// ... pass it around as you please - once you're ready to use it ...
c.assign(".tmp", r);
c.eval("useItAgain(.tmp)");
c.eval("rm(.tmp)")

NOTE: JRI 0.4-2 and earlier had a bug in that the referenced object in  
R was not preserved, so it could be garbage-collected between eval and  
the moment you assign it if you run additional R code (it was sort of  
deliberate for efficiency and voidEval but that's a long story). This  
was fixed/changed in 0.4-3, so please make sure you get the latest JRI/ 
rJava from RForge.net (rJava 0.6-3 or rJava 0.7-0 from today).

I hope it helps.

Cheers,
Simon

set PATH=%PATH%;C:\PROGRA~1\R\R-28~1.0\bin

Djava.library.path=C:\PROGRA~1\R\R-28~1.0\library\rJava\jri rtest

cat(gsub("/","\\\\",system.file("jri",package="rJava")),"\n")

Jannis,

this seems like an encoding mismatch issue to me. Java uses UTF-8  
encoding, so you must make sure that R is run in a UTF-8 locale. If   
that's not the case then you must convert any non-UTF8 strings to  
UTF-8 on the Java boundaries and vice versa. In most cases recent  
rJava/jri will perform the conversion for you if the R string has a  
known encoding, but there are pure C-level APIs that don't have such  
facilities (no encoding flag). The bottom line is that I'm pretty sure  
that this is a setting issue and you may want to look in the archives  
for encoding-related discussions.

Cheers,
Simon

> JRI.  So what would you recommend in such a case ?
>


Good question ;). For quite some time I was planning for both Rserve  
and JRI to have the same interface. In fact the new REngine-based  
client in Rserve is the new interface that was designed to be also  
compatible with JRI.

Now, finally, I have implemented it - so you can now use either JRI or  
Rserve transparently without any changes to your code. In fact I have  
taken the test class from Rserve and run it with JRI to make sure  
everything works as designed.

You will need the latest sources for this. What I recommend is using  
them from SVN as follows:

svn co svn://svn.rforge.net/org/trunk/rosuda/REngine
svn co svn://svn.rforge.net/org/trunk/rosuda/JRI

Then first prepare JRI (if you are on unix, just run
cd JRI
R CMD ./configure
make
cd ..

This should create the native library and JRI.jar then build REngine  
and its JRI part:
cd REngine
make
cd JRI
make
(to test, you can do cd test; make )

Alternatively you can compile JRIEngine.java with installed JRI, but  
make sure you have JRI 0.5 or later.

Cheers,
Simon

> the problem is this bean can only run at the first time,but failed

That is as expected - you can use only one R instance is one JVM,  
hence you can run new Rengine(..) only once in a Java VM. This is due  
to design limitations of R which doesn't not allow multiple threads.

If you need parallel processing, you may be better off using Rserve.  
Alternatively you can start multiple JVMs and use things like RMI, but  
that may be a bit too complex fro the task.

Cheers,
Simon
